entries.title: French at a glance
body: French is a Romance language, descended from Latin, and an official language in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada and many countries in Africa. The subject pronoun stays in the sentence: je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles.
Many final consonants are silent, and an -e on an adjective often marks the feminine in writing even when you cannot hear it.

entries.title: CEFR levels: what the official descriptions say
body: French courses and exams use the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), which has six levels: A1 and A2 (basic user), B1 and B2 (independent user), C1 and C2 (proficient user). The table quotes the first sentence of each level from the Council of Europe's global scale.
DELF covers A1 to B2 and DALF covers C1 and C2, both from France Éducation international, which also runs the TCF.

The CEFR describes what a learner can do with the language, not which grammar or words to learn, so the grammar column and the levels on this app's grammar are estimates. A range such as A2–B1 means a point commonly turns up at both levels.
Source: Council of Europe, Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (2001), global scale. The copyright of the scale belongs to the Council of Europe.

entries.title: Accents and silent letters
body: é is like the vowel in “say” without the glide. è and ê are more open, like “bed”. ç is an s before a, o, u: français. A final consonant is often silent (parlent sounds like parle), unless the next word begins with a vowel and the consonant is linked across (liaison).

head: Spelling
Roughly
rows: at the back of the throat

entries.title: le, la, les, un, une
entries.body: Nouns are masculine or feminine. le and la become l' before a vowel sound. After ne…pas, “a” or “some” becomes de.

entries.title: être, avoir, and -er verbs
entries.body: être and avoir are irregular and extremely common. Most other new verbs you meet at the start end in -er and follow parler.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: Seize is sixteen. From seventeen the pattern is dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, then vingt. In France, 70, 80 and 90 are built on vingt (soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix). Belgium and Switzerland use septante, huitante or octante, and nonante.

examples.e: I am twenty (literally “I have twenty years”)

entries.title: Please, thanks, and the bill
entries.body: s'il vous plaît is the polite “please”; s'il te plaît is for someone you call tu. merci is “thank you”, de rien or je vous en prie answers it. The café bill is l'addition.

entries.title: tu and vous
entries.body: vous is the safe choice with strangers, in shops, and at work. tu is for friends, family, children, and anyone who has invited you to use it. Switching is a small social step; if you are unsure, stay with vous.
